question_results.response:
[WHY_NOT]

Short answer
- There’s no explicit rule forbidding both column 1 and 6. The optimizer didn’t pick both because all feed (250 units) can be handled by a single first-stage column, and adding a second column only adds its fixed/amortized cost with no variable-cost benefit. In short: no capacity need + fixed-cost penalty = only one is used.

1) Which constraints made both unnecessary (plain language)
- Total throughput is fixed (F_tot = 250). With no per-column capacity below 250, any single first-stage column can handle the whole feed.
- Activation links: F[j] ≤ F_tot · y[j]. If y[j] = 0 → F[j] = 0. But if y[j] = 1, the model is not required to put any minimum flow on it (no min-flow constraint). So turning a column on does not force flow; the model will not pay for an extra column unless it reduces cost elsewhere.
- Stage-coupling and Q1 definitions (Q1[j] = K·F[j], sum q = Q1, etc.) don’t create a reason to split the 250 units across two columns when costs per unit are linear.
- Conclusion: the logical linking and balances make it possible and cheaper to process all flow in a single cheapest column.

2) Marginal evidence and practical proxies (numerical)
I ran targeted forced-on variants to quantify the cost impact:

- Baseline (optimal): y[3] = 1, y[21] = 1
  - F[3] = 250 → Q1[3] = 750; F[21] = 150 → Q1[21] = 450
  - Objective = 107,124.7411

- Force y[1] = 1 (allow re-optimization):
  - Model chooses y[1] = 1, y[21] = 1; F[1] = 250; objective = 107,772.0765
  - Penalty vs baseline: +647.3354 (using column 1 instead of column 3 is slightly worse)

- Force y[6] = 1:
  - Model chooses y[6] = 1, y[21] = 1; F[6] = 250; objective = 113,152.7583
  - Penalty vs baseline: +6,028.0172 (column 6 is much worse for the same throughput)

- Force y[1] = 1 and y[6] = 1 together:
  - Model sets F[1] = 250, F[6] = 0 (no flow to the second column) and y[21] = 1
  - Objective = 119,772.0765
  - Penalty vs y[1]-only: +12,000 exactly — this equals FC/alpha (30,000 / 2.5). That is the amortized fixed cost of turning on an extra column with zero flow.

Interpretation:
- Replacing the chosen first-stage column (3) with column 1 costs ~+647; with column 6 costs ~+6,028.
- Adding a second idle column costs exactly FC/alpha = 12,000 in objective, so the model assigns it zero flow rather than pay that cost for no benefit.

3) What-if changes to make both columns appear (practical suggestions)
To have both column 1 and 6 active in an optimal solution, you need either a capacity constraint or an economic incentive:

Capacity-based options:
- Impose a per-column max flow for first-stage columns, e.g., F[j] ≤ 150·y[j]. With F_tot = 250 this forces at least two columns.

Economic options (make splitting beneficial):
- Reduce the fixed cost burden:
  - Increase alpha (longer amortization) from 2.5 to a higher value (e.g., 10) so FC/alpha drops (30,000/10 = 3,000).
  - Or reduce FC directly (e.g., from 30,000 to ~5,000) so the amortized extra-column cost is much smaller.
- Improve heat-integration economics for columns 1 and 6:
  - Increase their temperature driving forces (bigger ΔT) or lower the area/heat-exchange cost multiplier for pairs involving these columns so splitting flow reduces exchanger capital enough to offset fixed cost.
  - Increase cooling-water cost (C_cu) significantly so process–process matches become more attractive, potentially making two columns cheaper in aggregate.
- Allow additional favorable matches in Stream_Matrix so columns 1 and 6 can use better temperature matches that reduce exchanger area.

4) Concrete numeric guidance
- The amortized fixed-cost of adding a second idle column is FC/alpha = 30,000 / 2.5 = 12,000. Any variable-cost saving from splitting must exceed ~12,000 to justify a second column.
- Substituting column 1 for the baseline costs ~+647; substituting column 6 costs ~+6,028. So with current parameters it’s always cheaper to use column 3 alone than to involve 1 or 6 in addition.
- To force both to appear without capacity limits, you need parameter changes that generate at least ~12,000 of variable-cost saving (e.g., large enough ΔT improvements or big increases in utility costs).

Bottom line
- The model favors a single first-stage column because it can handle the full throughput and adding another column only creates an amortized fixed-cost penalty with no saving. To see both columns selected, introduce either per-column capacity limits or change cost/temperature parameters to produce variable-cost savings greater than the 12,000 amortized fixed cost.

Would you like me to:
- run a what-if where I impose a per-column cap (e.g., 150) so two columns are required and show the new solution; or
- try reducing FC or increasing alpha to see when both columns become economical?
question_results.expert_response:
Short answer up front
- There is no explicit “at most one” constraint on columns 1 and 6. They don’t both appear because:
  1) all 250 units of feed can be handled by a single “first‑stage” column (no capacity limit per column), and
  2) turning on an extra column adds a fixed capital charge with no variable-cost benefit (costs are linear in flow, and there’s no minimum-flow requirement once a column is selected).
- Forcing one or both on confirms this: column 1 is a small penalty vs the baseline option, column 6 is a bigger penalty, and turning both on just adds the fixed cost of an idle extra column.

Details

1) Which constraints/bounds made both 1 and 6 unnecessary
- Total throughput is fixed by mass balance: sum of flows over the ABC front-end set equals F_tot = 250. With no per-column capacity smaller than 250, one first-stage column can process the entire 250.
  - Code: sum(F[j] for j in F_subset) == F_tot; here F_tot = 250.
- Logical link between selection and flow is one-way only: F[j] ≤ F_tot·y[j].
  - If y[j] = 0, F[j] must be 0. But if y[j] = 1, the model is not required to send any flow to that column (there is no minimum-flow constraint). So the optimizer can switch a column “on” and still assign it zero flow.
- Stage-coupling (split) constraints fix downstream needs given first‑stage flow, so only one first‑stage column is required:
  - 0.6 × (sum of first‑stage flows) = (sum of last‑stage flows)
  - 0.9 × (sum of AB/C flows) = (sum of A/B flows)
  In all solutions we solved, the first-stage flow stays at 250, which forces the last-stage flow sum to 150. That single downstream requirement is met by one downstream column (column 21 in all cases). This again removes any incentive to split the first-stage flow across two columns.
- Heat flow matching constraints simply reconcile condenser/reboiler duties with exchanger assignments; they don’t force multiple first‑stage columns either:
  - Q1[j] = K·F[j] (K = 3)
  - For each hot index j: sum_i q[i,j] = QH[j] = Q1[j]
  - For each cold index i: sum_j q[i,j] = QC[i] = Q1[i]
  These don’t introduce a benefit from “two” first‑stage columns when the costs are linear.

Net effect: with linear variable costs and no per‑column capacity < 250 or minimum-flow requirement, the model pushes all 250 units through a single cheapest first‑stage option and avoids paying an extra fixed cost to turn on a second one.

2) Marginal evidence (objective changes when we force choices)
We solved four cases to quantify the penalty/benefit:

- Baseline optimal (unconstrained):
  - Selected columns: y[3] = 1 and y[21] = 1
  - Flows/duties: F[3] = 250 → Q1[3] = 750; F[21] = 150 → Q1[21] = 450
  - Objective = 107124.7411

- Force y[1] = 1 (let the model re-optimize everything else):
  - Selected: y[1] = 1, y[21] = 1 (column 3 is dropped)
  - Flows/duties: F[1] = 250 → Q1[1] = 750; F[21] = 150 → Q1[21] = 450
  - Objective = 107772.0765 (penalty vs baseline: +647.3354)
  Interpretation: using col 1 instead of col 3 is slightly worse (about +0.6%). The full 250 still goes through a single first‑stage column (now #1), and the 150 still goes through column 21. The small penalty comes from heat‑exchanger/utility terms (temperature match differences); fixed costs and linear variable costs cancel in substitution.

- Force y[6] = 1:
  - Selected: y[6] = 1, y[21] = 1 (column 3 is dropped)
  - Flows/duties: F[6] = 250 → Q1[6] = 750; F[21] = 150 → Q1[21] = 450
  - Objective = 113152.7583 (penalty vs baseline: +6028.0172)
  Interpretation: column 6 is much more expensive than column 3 for the same throughput (about +5.6%), again due to heat‑exchange (poorer temperature differences mean larger area cost or less favorable utility use).

- Force both y[1] = 1 and y[6] = 1:
  - Selected: y[1] = 1, y[6] = 1, y[21] = 1
  - Flows/duties: F[1] = 250 → Q1[1] = 750; F[6] = 0 → Q1[6] = 0; F[21] = 150 → Q1[21] = 450
  - Objective = 119772.0765 (penalty vs y[1]-only: +12000.0000)
  Interpretation: the model keeps all flow on column 1 and assigns zero to column 6. The objective increase is exactly the amortized fixed cost of adding one more column: FC/alpha = 30000 / 2.5 = 12000. There is no variable-cost benefit to splitting the flow, so the second column just adds fixed cost.

Practical “marginal” proxies:
- Substituting column 1 for column 3 costs about +647 (per year-equivalent with alpha=2.5).
- Substituting column 6 for column 3 costs about +6028.
- Turning on an additional idle first-stage column at the y[1]-only solution costs exactly +12000 (the amortized fixed cost); this is the effective reduced cost of “adding a redundant first-stage column.”

3) What-if levers to make both columns appear
If your real goal is to see both first‑stage columns present in the optimal plan, you need to either:
- Create a capacity reason to split the flow; or
- Create an economic reason (variable-cost savings) that outweighs the extra fixed cost of a second column.

A few concrete options (with values):
- Add/ tighten per-column capacity so one column cannot do all 250:
  - Replace F[j] ≤ F_tot·y[j] with F[j] ≤ 150·y[j] for first-stage columns. With F_tot = 250, the model would need at least two first‑stage columns active. In practice, you could introduce a new parameter F_cap_first = 150 and apply it to j in the first‑stage set (which includes columns 1 and 6).
- Reduce (or amortize over longer time) the fixed cost so a second column’s “penalty” is small:
  - Currently FC/alpha = 12000. If you double the payout time alpha from 2.5 to, say, 10, the added cost per extra column drops to 3000. That’s closer to the observed variable-cost gaps and makes it easier for the model to justify a second column if any small variable-cost advantage appears.
  - Alternatively, lower FC from 30000 to around 5000; then FC/alpha = 2000. Note: even at zero fixed cost the model still won’t add a redundant column unless there’s a variable-cost advantage or a tie; free but unused capacity is still not chosen by an optimizer that minimizes cost.
- Make heat integration materially cheaper/ more attractive for columns 1 and 6 so splitting flow reduces exchanger/utility costs by ≥ FC (30,000, since hex_cost shares the same 1/alpha scaling as FC in the objective):
  - Increase the condenser temperatures for cols 1 and 6 (cond_hot_temp[1] and cond_hot_temp[6]) by ~10–15 K or reduce the target reboiler temperatures they would heat (reb_cold_temp for the matching cold indices) by a similar amount. That raises the temperature difference, cuts area, and can flip the economics toward using two hot streams.
  - Increase the cooling-water cost C_cu by 5–10x (e.g., from 1.59e-07 to ~1.0e-06). Today, both condenser duties are dumped to cooling water; making that expensive nudges the solver to favor process–process matches. If columns 1 and 6 provide two hot condensers that can cover two different reboilers well, the utility and area savings can justify a second column.
  - Reduce the area-cost coefficient (the “300” multiplier) specifically for process–process pairs involving columns 1 and 6 (if that’s physically reasonable), which would make their integration cheaper than the current baseline option.

4) Numerical evidence from the solved runs
- Baseline optimal:
  - y[3] = 1, y[21] = 1; y[1] = 0, y[6] = 0
  - F[3] = 250 → Q1[3] = 750; F[21] = 150 → Q1[21] = 450
  - Objective = 107124.7411
- Force y[1] = 1:
  - y[1] = 1, y[21] = 1; F[1] = 250 → Q1[1] = 750; F[21] = 150 → Q1[21] = 450
  - Objective = 107772.0765 (Δ +647.3354 vs baseline)
- Force y[6] = 1:
  - y[6] = 1, y[21] = 1; F[6] = 250 → Q1[6] = 750; F[21] = 150 → Q1[21] = 450
  - Objective = 113152.7583 (Δ +6028.0172 vs baseline)
- Force y[1] = 1 and y[6] = 1 together:
  - y[1] = 1, y[6] = 1, y[21] = 1; F[1] = 250, F[6] = 0; Q1[1] = 750, Q1[6] = 0; F[21] = 150 → Q1[21] = 450
  - Objective = 119772.0765 (Δ +12000.0000 vs y[1]-only, pure fixed-cost hit)

Plain-language takeaway
- The model funnels the whole 250 units through a single first‑stage column because it’s allowed to and it’s cheapest. Adding a second first‑stage column creates no savings (costs are linear in flow, and cooling water/steam choices remain the same), but it does add a fixed cost of 12,000 per year-equivalent. That’s why the optimizer does not pick y[1] = 1 and y[6] = 1 at the same time.
- To see both appear, you need either a capacity reason (per-column cap below 250) or stronger heat-integration economics that make the variable-cost savings from running two first-stage columns exceed the 12,000 amortized fixed cost.

It also provides a coherent optimization reason (extra fixed/amortized cost with no need/capacity benefit) and does not contradict feasibility or optimality claims.

What the model actually did (key variables)
- Opened centers: Y[2] = 1, Y[3] = 1, Y[4] = 1. Centers 0 and 1 remain closed (Y[0] = 0, Y[1] = 0).

Why that combination is cheaper (main drivers)
1. Fixed opening cost f[i]:

   - f[3] ≈ 1,065,020.51; f[4] ≈ 1,099,555.05.
   - f[0] and f[1] are larger (f[0] ≈ 1,617,567.50; f[1] ≈ 1,129,760.19).

2. Capacity fit cc[i]:

   - Residual after 3 and 4: ≈ 1,855.7 units; cc[2] ≈ 1,880.26 — a near-perfect fit (2 can take the leftover without needing another site).
   Because 2’s capacity closely matches the leftover requirement, the solution avoids opening additional expensive capacity.

3. Inbound shipping costs c[k,i] and routing:
   - The model routes significant flows from several zones to center 2 (see X[3,2], X[6,2], X[7,2], X[8,2]). That indicates c[k,2] is competitive for those k’s, so shipping + fixed cost is low overall.

Relevant constraints
- constraint_2 (flow balance): All returns from each zone k must be assigned to some center: sum_i X[k,i] = r[k].
- constraint_7 (center capacity): sum_k X[k,i] ≤ cc[i]·Y[i] — a center can only accept flow if opened and up to its capacity.
